topic: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) and the Rule of Five
explanation: RAII is a fundamental C++ programming technique that tightly couples resource management with object lifetime.  It ensures that resources (like dynamically allocated memory, files, network connections, etc.) are automatically acquired when an object is created and released when the object is destroyed, even in the face of exceptions.  The Rule of Five dictates that if you define any of the special member functions (copy constructor, copy assignment operator, move constructor, move assignment operator, or destructor), you should explicitly define *all* of them to prevent subtle bugs and resource leaks.  Failing to do so can lead to double deletion, memory leaks, or other undefined behavior.
code_example: HasPtr(const std::string& s = std::string{}) : ps(std::make_unique<std::string>(s)), i(0) {}
//Copy/Move constructors and assignment operators are implicitly defined and handled efficiently by unique_ptr
HasPtr hp2 = hp1; //Uses implicitly defined copy constructor
example_explanation: This improved example uses `std::unique_ptr` which simplifies RAII and eliminates the need for explicit copy/move constructors and assignment operators. `unique_ptr` automatically manages the memory deallocation in the destructor, preventing memory leaks. This approach is safer and more idiomatic in modern C++ than manual memory management.  It demonstrates how smart pointers greatly enhance RAII, making code cleaner, safer, and more maintainable.  The Rule of Five still applies conceptually; the compiler generates the special member functions for us, but understanding the principles behind it is crucial for working with classes managing resources.
